patient.name: Kwame Asante
patient.setting: Emergency Department (sent in by his GP)
patient.complaint: Three months of tiredness, two chest infections and new bruising; feverish today
background: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy 6 years ago, in remission
Retired bus driver from Lewisham, lives with his wife

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with low Hb, WCC and platelets: the film (blasts, hyposegmented neutrophils), the MCV, the drug history and the marrow cellularity decide the cause.

points: Kwame, 71, tired and **breathless on stairs** for 3 months.
Two chest infections since the summer, each slow to clear.
Bruises he cannot explain; two **nosebleeds** this month.
Since this morning: shivers and feeling hot.

steps.lead: Three problems at once, anaemia, infections and bleeding, means all **three cell lines** are low: that is pancytopenia.
Kwame is **older** and had **chemotherapy and radiotherapy** for lymphoma: both put him at risk.
Each symptom maps to one line: tiredness (**red cells**), infections (**white cells**), bruising and nosebleeds (**platelets**). Kwame's exam shows pallor, bruising and fever.

steps.title: One cell line, one symptom
nodes: All three together → think bone marrow
steps.caption: When all three are low, the problem is usually the factory (marrow), not the blood.

steps.q: Kwame is pancytopenic with a temperature of 38.4°C. What must you assume?
steps.r: Pancytopenia plus fever is **neutropenic sepsis** until proven otherwise: a medical emergency needing IV antibiotics within the hour.

steps.lead: Kwame's fever is the danger sign: he is treated as **neutropenic sepsis** while the cause of his low counts is worked out.
Kwame's past **chemotherapy** makes therapy-related **MDS** or acute leukaemia high on the list; a drug cause and B12 deficiency must also be excluded.

steps.text: A raised MCV with pancytopenia is not always B12 or folate. In an older patient after chemotherapy, **MDS** also gives a **macrocytic** anaemia.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?': FBC and blood film come first, but bone marrow biopsy is the test that confirms the cause.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods
steps.text: All three lines low with a high MCV; B12 and folate are normal.

steps.lead: Kwame's **FBC** shows the reduction in all three lines; next the **blood film** looks for abnormal cells.

visual.title: Neutrophil count
visual.label: Kwame 0.4
visual.caption: Below 0.5 with a fever: neutropenic sepsis.

steps.q: The film suggests a marrow cause. Which test confirms it?
steps.r: **Bone marrow biopsy** (aspirate and trephine) is the gold standard: it shows cellularity, dysplasia, blasts or infiltration.

steps.lead: Kwame's **bone marrow biopsy** is booked once he is stable from his sepsis.

visual.title: Marrow blasts on biopsy
visual.label: Kwame 8%
visual.caption: Hypercellular, dysplastic marrow with 8% blasts and ringed sideroblasts: MDS, not yet AML.

steps.text: Low counts with a **hypercellular** marrow means **ineffective** production (MDS, leukaemia). Low counts with a **hypocellular** marrow means **failure** (aplastic anaemia).

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': fever means IV antibiotics now; otherwise support each cell line and treat the cause (transplant or immunosuppression for aplastic anaemia, chemotherapy for leukaemia, folic acid with methotrexate).

points: IV **piperacillin with tazobactam** given within the hour.

steps.q: What is the most important first step for Kwame?
o: Oral amoxicillin and review in 48 hours
steps.r: Neutropenic sepsis kills fast: **empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour** (NICE). The biopsy can wait until he is stable.

steps.lead: Kwame needs **support for each line**: antibiotics for the infection, red cells for his Hb of 78 and platelets if he bleeds, while the cause is found.

visual.title: Kwame's first week
visual.caption: Transfusions lift his counts only for days: support buys time, but the marrow cause still needs treating.

steps.title: Pancytopenia: management
nodes: Fever? → neutropenic sepsis: IV antibiotics within 1 h
Support: red cells, platelets, infection control
Find the cause: film, B12/folate, drugs, marrow
steps.caption: Support first, then target the cause.

steps.lead: Kwame's long-term plan depends on his marrow: **MDS** is managed by haematology; **aplastic anaemia** would need immunosuppression or transplant.

steps.text: Anyone on **methotrexate** takes **folic acid** (weekly, on a different day) and has regular FBCs: methotrexate toxicity is a classic exam cause of pancytopenia.

steps.lead: Kwame's haematology team follows the **British Society for Haematology** guidance on aplastic anaemia and MDS.

steps.text: Do not delay antibiotics for a febrile neutropenic patient to get cultures back or a chest X-ray. Treat first; adjust later.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why the marrow is hypocellular in aplastic anaemia but hypercellular in MDS, and how methotrexate suppresses the marrow (dihydrofolate reductase).

steps.lead: Kwame's counts are low because his marrow is not making **normal** cells, through failure or replacement.
In **aplastic anaemia** the stem cells themselves are destroyed (autoimmune, drug or toxin), so the marrow is empty and fatty.
Kwame's marrow is **full**, yet his blood is empty: his dysplastic cells die **inside the marrow** before they are released.

steps.title: Why MDS gives a full marrow and empty blood
nodes: Clonal stem cell abnormality (e.g. after chemotherapy)

steps.q: Which enzyme does methotrexate inhibit to cause marrow suppression?
steps.r: Methotrexate blocks **dihydrofolate reductase**, so no tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is the B12 enzyme.

steps.lead: Kwame is not on methotrexate, but it is the drug the exam uses most: it starves dividing marrow precursors of **folate** for DNA synthesis.

o: Reduction in red cells, white cells and platelets
Raised white cells with low platelets
mcq.r: Pancytopenia is a reduction in **all three** cell lines.

mcq.q: A pancytopenic patient has a temperature of 38.5°C. What is this?
mcq.r: Pancytopenia plus fever = **neutropenic sepsis**, a medical emergency.

mcq.q: Which blood film finding suggests myelodysplastic syndrome?
mcq.r: **Pelger-Huët** hyposegmented neutrophils with a macrocytic anaemia point to MDS. Auer rods suggest AML.

mcq.q: Which anticonvulsant is a recognised cause of aplastic anaemia?
mcq.r: The notes list **phenytoin** (and methotrexate) as causes of aplastic anaemia.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard investigation for pancytopenia?
mcq.r: **Bone marrow biopsy** confirms the cause; FBC and film come first.

mcq.q: Which marrow finding fits aplastic anaemia?
mcq.r: Aplastic anaemia: **hypocellular, fatty** marrow. Ringed sideroblasts suggest MDS.

mcq.q: What should be co-prescribed with methotrexate?
mcq.r: **Folic acid** reduces methotrexate marrow toxicity; FBCs are monitored too.

mcq.q: Which is a definitive treatment option for severe aplastic anaemia?
mcq.r: Aplastic anaemia: **immunosuppression or bone marrow transplant**.

mcq.q: Why is the marrow hypercellular in MDS despite low blood counts?
o: Ineffective, dysplastic maturation with cell death in the marrow
mcq.r: MDS cells mature abnormally and die **inside the marrow** (ineffective haematopoiesis).
**DHFR** inhibition blocks tetrahydrofolate, so DNA synthesis in dividing cells fails.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has 4 months of fatigue and two chest infections. He had chemotherapy for lymphoma 5 years ago. He has pallor and bruising but no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. A blood film shows macrocytes and neutrophils with bilobed nuclei.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about pancytopenia: use the film, the MCV and the history to pick the marrow cause.
Older, previous chemo, macrocytic pancytopenia and **Pelger-Huët** neutrophils; normal B12; no organomegaly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Macrocytic pancytopenia with hyposegmented neutrophils after chemotherapy: **myelodysplastic syndrome**.

elim: AML shows **blasts** on the film and a rapid course.
Aplastic anaemia is normocytic with no dysplastic cells.
Myelofibrosis gives massive splenomegaly and teardrop cells.
B12 is normal and B12 deficiency would not give bilobed neutrophils.

steps.x: **C. Myelodysplastic syndrome.** Rule: macrocytic pancytopenia + Pelger-Huët in an older patient = MDS.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman has 2 months of tiredness and easy bruising. She has pallor and scattered petechiae. A blood film shows no blasts. Serum B12 and folate are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' means the test that confirms the cause, not the first test.
Pancytopenia with the simple causes (B12, folate) excluded: the marrow must be examined.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bone marrow biopsy**, the gold standard.

elim: CT stages lymphoma or cancer but does not explain the marrow.
DAT is for haemolysis; it does not explain low white cells and platelets.
B12 is normal, so pernicious anaemia testing is not needed.
Repeating the FBC delays diagnosis; the result is already clear.

steps.x: **A. Bone marrow biopsy.** FBC and film first; biopsy confirms.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man is having chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia. He has had rigors for 3 hours. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management: what saves his life in the next hour?
Neutrophils 0.2 with fever and tachycardia: **neutropenic sepsis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Empirical broad-spectrum **IV antibiotics** within 1 hour: piperacillin with tazobactam.

elim: A biopsy does not treat sepsis.
Oral narrow-spectrum antibiotics are inadequate in neutropenic sepsis.
Platelets of 28 with no bleeding do not need urgent transfusion.
Hb 86 is not the immediate threat.

steps.x: **B. IV piperacillin with tazobactam.** Pancytopenia + fever = antibiotics within the hour.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man has had petechiae and fatigue for 3 weeks. He started phenytoin 2 months ago. Blood film shows no abnormal cells. Bone marrow trephine shows a markedly hypocellular marrow replaced by fat.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his pancytopenia?
o: Clonal dysplastic maturation of myeloid cells
Impaired thymidine synthesis from B12 deficiency

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the marrow appearance.
Drug exposure and an **empty, fatty** marrow: aplastic anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Aplastic anaemia: drug or immune-mediated **destruction of haematopoietic stem cells**.

elim: Dysplasia (MDS) gives a hypercellular marrow.
B12 deficiency gives a megaloblastic, cellular marrow.
Infiltration would show blasts and a full marrow.
Sequestration needs splenomegaly and leaves the marrow active.

steps.x: **B. Destruction of haematopoietic stem cells.** Hypocellular = failure; hypercellular = ineffective or infiltrated.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman has 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness. She had radiotherapy for breast cancer 8 years ago. She has pallor and a few bruises; there is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. A blood film shows hyposegmented neutrophils.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Macrocytic pancytopenia with hyposegmented (Pelger-Huët) neutrophils in an older woman after radiotherapy is MDS. B12 and folate are normal, and aplastic anaemia is normocytic.

steps.x: Diagnosis: which cause of pancytopenia?

clues: radiotherapy for breast cancer 8 years ago
steps.x: Prior radiotherapy, older age, Pelger-Huët cells, macrocytosis, normal haematinics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myelodysplastic syndrome**.

elim: ALL is mainly in children and shows lymphoblasts.
Aplastic anaemia is normocytic with no dysplasia.
Folate is normal.
Myelofibrosis gives massive splenomegaly; there is none.

steps.x: **D. MDS.** Older + prior chemo/radiotherapy + macrocytic + Pelger-Huët.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has 3 weeks of fatigue, nosebleeds and a petechial rash. He started carbamazepine 6 weeks ago. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. The blood film shows no abnormal cells and the reticulocyte count is low.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A young man with normocytic pancytopenia, low reticulocytes, no abnormal cells and a new anticonvulsant has drug-induced aplastic anaemia. ITP affects platelets alone.

steps.x: Diagnosis: young patient, three lines low.
New anticonvulsant, normocytic, empty-looking film, marrow not responding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drug-induced **aplastic anaemia** (marrow failure).

elim: AML would show blasts.
Haemolysis gives a high reticulocyte count and normal white cells.
ITP lowers platelets only; Hb and neutrophils are normal.
MDS is a disease of older people, with macrocytosis and dysplasia.

steps.x: **B. Aplastic anaemia.** Normocytic pancytopenia + low retics + drug = marrow failure.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with myelodysplastic syndrome has felt shivery for 4 hours. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. He has no cough, urinary symptoms or rash.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever with a neutrophil count below 0.5 in a pancytopenic patient is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; there may be no focal source because neutrophils are needed to make pus and signs.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what is happening now?

clues: no cough, urinary symptoms or rash
steps.x: Pancytopenia, fever, hypotension, raised lactate; no focus is typical when neutrophils are absent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Neutropenic sepsis**.

elim: PE gives pleuritic pain and hypoxia, not rigors with neutropenia.
Transformation needs a rising blast count, not acute fever.
He has not been transfused.
Hypotension and raised lactate are not a simple viral cold.

steps.x: **A. Neutropenic sepsis.** Pancytopenia + fever = emergency.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has 2 weeks of mouth ulcers, bruising and a sore throat. She takes weekly methotrexate. She stopped her other weekly tablet a month ago because it 'seemed unnecessary'. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her pancytopenia?
practice.e: She stopped her folic acid, so methotrexate (a DHFR inhibitor) is suppressing her marrow: macrocytic pancytopenia with mouth ulcers. Felty's needs splenomegaly; anaemia of chronic disease does not lower all three lines.

steps.x: Cause question: what has changed?
The other weekly tablet is **folic acid**; mouth ulcers and macrocytic pancytopenia are methotrexate toxicity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Methotrexate marrow toxicity** after stopping folic acid.

elim: Felty's needs splenomegaly and causes mainly neutropenia.
Myelofibrosis gives massive splenomegaly and a dry tap.
Pernicious anaemia does not explain the timing after stopping folate.
Anaemia of chronic disease is normocytic and spares white cells and platelets.

steps.x: **B. Methotrexate toxicity.** Always co-prescribe folic acid and monitor the FBC.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has had fatigue and recurrent infections for 4 months. He had chemotherapy 6 years ago. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. FBC shows pancytopenia with an MCV of 107 fL. B12 and folate are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on bone marrow biopsy?
o: Hypercellular marrow with dysplasia and ringed sideroblasts
practice.e: Macrocytic pancytopenia after chemotherapy in an older man is MDS: a hypercellular, dysplastic marrow with ringed sideroblasts. A hypocellular marrow would be aplastic anaemia.

steps.x: Finding question: what will the marrow show?
Therapy-related, macrocytic, haematinics normal: MDS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: MDS marrow: **hypercellular, dysplastic**, ringed sideroblasts.

elim: A dry tap is myelofibrosis, which needs splenomegaly.
Hypocellular is aplastic anaemia, which is normocytic.
No primary cancer history to suggest metastasis.
Increased megakaryocytes with normal marrow fits ITP, not pancytopenia.

steps.x: **B. Hypercellular and dysplastic.** Low blood counts with a full marrow = ineffective haematopoiesis.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has 2 weeks of bleeding gums, fatigue and fevers. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. He has gum hypertrophy and petechiae. A blood film shows many large immature cells containing Auer rods.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Rapid-onset pancytopenia with myeloid blasts containing Auer rods and gum infiltration is AML, a marrow infiltration cause of pancytopenia. MDS has fewer than 20% blasts and no rapid course.

steps.x: Diagnosis: which marrow infiltration?
Fast onset, gum infiltration and **Auer rods** in blasts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **AML** crowding out normal haematopoiesis.

elim: Aplastic anaemia has no abnormal cells.
CLL raises the lymphocyte count with smear cells.
MDS is slower, without circulating Auer-rod blasts.
B12 deficiency does not produce blasts.

steps.x: **A. AML.** Blasts with Auer rods = AML.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has 2 months of fatigue and bruising. He has pallor and petechiae. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Blood film shows macrocytes and hypogranular neutrophils. Serum B12 and folate are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Bone marrow biopsy is the gold standard for pancytopenia and will confirm MDS. B12 is normal, so intrinsic factor antibodies add nothing.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: the confirming test.
Dysplastic film, haematinics normal: the marrow must be sampled.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bone marrow biopsy**.

elim: CT looks for lymphoma or cancer but cannot diagnose a marrow disorder.
Electrophoresis is for haemoglobinopathies.
Normal B12 makes pernicious anaemia unlikely.
Ferritin assesses iron, which causes microcytic anaemia only.

steps.x: **A. Bone marrow biopsy.**

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has 3 weeks of tiredness, bruising and two episodes of tonsillitis. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. She has pallor and petechiae on her legs. She takes no regular medicines.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Full blood count and blood film
practice.e: The first-line test is the FBC, which shows the reduction in all three lines, and the blood film, which may show abnormal cells. Marrow biopsy follows to confirm the cause.

steps.x: Initial investigation: the first test, not the confirming one.

clues: tiredness, bruising and two episodes of tonsillitis
steps.x: Symptoms of all three lines failing: anaemia, infection, bleeding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **FBC and blood film** first.

elim: Biopsy is diagnostic but comes after the FBC.
Imaging before a blood count is premature.
Monospot tests for glandular fever but does not assess the cell lines.
Ferritin only assesses iron stores.

steps.x: **C. FBC and film.** FBC first; biopsy confirms.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has just finished her third cycle of chemotherapy for lymphoma. She has had rigors for 2 hours. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Blood cultures have been taken.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Neutropenic sepsis needs empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour (piperacillin with tazobactam). Waiting for cultures or imaging delays life-saving treatment.

steps.x: Next step: cultures are done, so what now?
Neutrophils 0.2 with fever after chemotherapy: **neutropenic sepsis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV piperacillin with tazobactam** now.

elim: Waiting for cultures risks death.
A CXR must not delay antibiotics.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate for neutropenic sepsis.
Platelets of 60 without bleeding need no transfusion.

steps.x: **C. IV piperacillin with tazobactam.**

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has severe aplastic anaemia confirmed on bone marrow biopsy, with no drug cause found. He has needed red cell and platelet transfusions every week. His brother is a fully HLA-matched donor. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Aplastic anaemia is treated with immunosuppression or bone marrow transplant; a young patient with a matched sibling donor is offered transplant. Transfusion alone is only supportive.

steps.x: Long-term management: definitive, not supportive.
Young, severe, and a matched sibling: ideal for transplant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Allogeneic bone marrow transplant**.

elim: B12 is for B12 deficiency.
Transfusions support but do not cure, and cause iron overload.
Folic acid treats folate deficiency, not stem cell failure.
Splenectomy does not restore marrow production.

steps.x: **A. Bone marrow transplant.** Older or no donor: immunosuppression instead.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is starting weekly methotrexate. She has no other medical problems. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional prescription to reduce her risk of pancytopenia?
practice.e: Methotrexate patients are co-prescribed folic acid and have FBC monitoring for anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia and marrow suppression.

steps.x: Prevention: which drug protects her marrow?
Methotrexate blocks folate metabolism and can suppress the marrow.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Folic acid**, on a different day from methotrexate.

elim: B12 does not reverse DHFR inhibition.
Iron does not protect against marrow suppression.
Omeprazole protects the stomach, not the marrow.
Prednisolone is not a marrow protector.

steps.x: **C. Folic acid.** Plus regular FBCs.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has mouth ulcers and bruising. She has been taking methotrexate daily instead of weekly. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 126/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her pancytopenia?
o: Autoimmune destruction of platelets in the spleen
Infiltration of the marrow by plasma cells
Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase in marrow precursors
practice.e: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking tetrahydrofolate synthesis for DNA, so rapidly dividing marrow precursors fail. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is the B12-dependent enzyme.

steps.x: Mechanism: how does this drug cause it?
Methotrexate overdose: rapidly dividing cells (mouth, marrow) fail.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DHFR inhibition** blocking DNA synthesis.

elim: That is ITP, affecting platelets only.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs B12, not affected by methotrexate.
Plasma cell infiltration is myeloma.
Reduced intrinsic factor is pernicious anaemia.

steps.x: **C. DHFR inhibition.** Folic acid (folinic acid in overdose) mitigates it.

Blood film may show abnormal cells

points.p: Aplastic anaemia: immunosuppression or bone marrow transplant

glossary.Pancytopenia: A reduction in all three blood cell lines: red cells, white cells and platelets.
glossary.Neutropenic sepsis: Fever or sepsis with a neutrophil count below 0.5 ×10⁹/L; an emergency needing IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
glossary.Neutropenia: A low neutrophil count, which raises the risk of bacterial and fungal infection.
glossary.Thrombocytopenia: A low platelet count, causing bruising, petechiae and bleeding.
glossary.Leukopenia: A low total white cell count.
glossary.Leucopenia: A low total white cell count (alternative spelling of leukopenia).
glossary.Petechiae: Pinpoint red or purple spots from bleeding into the skin, seen with low platelets.
glossary.Aplastic anaemia: Marrow failure from destruction of haematopoietic stem cells, giving a hypocellular, fatty marrow and pancytopenia.
glossary.MDS: Myelodysplastic syndrome: a clonal marrow disorder with ineffective, dysplastic blood cell production.
glossary.Myelodysplastic syndrome: A clonal stem cell disorder of older people causing dysplastic cells, cytopenias and risk of AML.
glossary.Pelger-Huët: Neutrophils with hyposegmented or bilobed nuclei; a classic film finding in MDS.
glossary.Ringed sideroblasts: Red cell precursors with iron-loaded mitochondria ringing the nucleus, seen on marrow iron stain in MDS.
glossary.AML: Acute myeloid leukaemia: rapid accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow.
glossary.Auer rods: Needle-shaped inclusions in myeloid blasts, typical of AML.
glossary.Blasts: Immature precursor cells; large numbers in blood or marrow suggest acute leukaemia.
glossary.Hypocellular: A marrow with too few blood-forming cells, replaced by fat; typical of aplastic anaemia.
glossary.Hypercellular: A marrow packed with cells; seen in MDS and leukaemia despite low blood counts.
glossary.Haematopoiesis: The production of blood cells from stem cells in the bone marrow.
glossary.Haematopoietic stem cells: Marrow stem cells that give rise to all blood cell lines.
glossary.Bone marrow biopsy: Sampling of marrow (aspirate and trephine) to assess cellularity and abnormal cells; the gold standard here.
glossary.Trephine: A core of bone marrow tissue taken with a biopsy needle to show marrow architecture.
glossary.Blood film: A stained smear of blood examined under the microscope to look at cell shape and abnormal cells.
glossary.Dry tap: A failed marrow aspirate because the marrow is fibrosed; classic of myelofibrosis.
glossary.Myelofibrosis: Marrow fibrosis causing a dry tap, teardrop cells and massive splenomegaly.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume: average red cell size; above 100 fL is macrocytic.
glossary.Macrocytic: Red cells larger than normal (MCV above 100 fL), seen in B12/folate deficiency and MDS.
glossary.Normocytic: Red cells of normal size (MCV 80 to 100 fL).
glossary.Reticulocyte: A young red cell; a low count means the marrow is not responding.
glossary.Methotrexate: An antimetabolite (DHFR inhibitor) used in rheumatoid arthritis and cancer that can suppress the marrow.
glossary.Dihydrofolate reductase: The enzyme that makes tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis; inhibited by methotrexate.
glossary.DHFR: Dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme blocked by methotrexate.
glossary.Tetrahydrofolate: The active form of folate needed to make DNA bases.
glossary.Folic acid: Folate supplement co-prescribed with methotrexate to reduce marrow toxicity.
glossary.Phenytoin: An anticonvulsant that is a recognised cause of aplastic anaemia.
glossary.Carbamazepine: An anticonvulsant that can cause marrow suppression and aplastic anaemia.
glossary.Piperacillin with tazobactam: A broad-spectrum IV antibiotic used first-line in neutropenic sepsis.
glossary.Immunosuppression: Drugs that dampen the immune system; used in aplastic anaemia to stop stem cell destruction.
glossary.Bone marrow transplant: Replacement of a failed or diseased marrow with donor stem cells.
glossary.HLA-matched: A donor whose tissue type matches the recipient, lowering rejection risk in transplant.
glossary.Felty's syndrome: Rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly and neutropenia.
glossary.Cytopenia: A low count of any one blood cell type.
